title-group.article-title: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader

p.bold: ABSTRACT Hybrid technologies are considered one of the key solutions for CO2 reduction in large off-highway machines that operate for long hours in suburban areas with limited access to energy refueling infrastructure. The effectiveness of CO2 reduction through hybridization largely depends on the hybrid powertrain architecture and its operating strategies. This paper uses a parallel-series hybrid wheel loader as a research platform to investigate and optimize energy management strategies. The parallel-series hybrid powertrain consists of a pure electric propulsion system and a parallel hybrid working hydraulic system. In this paper, a real-time capable energy management strategy based on an optimization theory is presented. This strategy combines Dynamic Programming (DP) and Pontryagin's Minimum Principle (PMP) to optimize both engine start-stop sequence and torque split between the engine and the electric machine, while balancing the disadvantages of each control theory. To enable real-time implementation of the proposed control strategy, short-term vehicle power demand is predicted using a state detection algorithm developed to account for the repetitive nature of the duty cycles of a wheel loader. Simulation results indicate that fuel consumption can be reduced by 4.0% compared to a rule-based strategy in a typical loading cycle. Test results with a prototype hybrid wheel loader confirm that the proposed control strategy operates in real-time and improves system efficiency. In particular, the average engine brake fuel consumption (BSFC) improved by 0.7% in the loading cycle and by 1.3% in a more realistic mission cycle that combines the loading cycle with driving.

sec.label: I.
sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: total EU27 GHG emissions [1], reducing CO2 emissions in this sector will have even greater significance in the future, as food production and construction demands are expected to rise with the growing world population. In this context, hybrid technologies have been attracting the attention of researchers and construction machinery manufacturers due to their onboard energy capacity and ease of refueling [31]. Several hybrid construction machines have already been developed in the past [2], [3], [4], [5]. The effectiveness of CO2 reduction through hybridization depends not only on the hybrid powertrain architecture, but also on its energy management strategies. An overview and

The global concern over climate change is pushing automotive manufacturers to reduce pollutant emissions from their products. Since pollutant emission limits for the off-highway sector have become more stringent, following the trend of on-highway vehicles, it is expected that even stricter emission standards will be introduced in the off-highway sector. Although greenhouse gases (GHG) emissions from the offhighway sector are estimated to account for only 2% of the

classification of energy management strategies developed for off-highway machines can be found in [6] and [7]. A primary distinction is made between rule-based and optimizationbased control strategies. In rule-based control strategies, control decisions are made based on predefined rules derived from prior knowledge of the system, operating conditions, and empirical experience. These strategies are often preferred for real-world vehicle implementation because of their low computational effort. For this reason, existing hybrid construction machines primarily adopt rule-based strategies [6], and extensive research has been conducted in this area. In [8], a rule-based strategy was developed for an excavator equipped with a parallel hybrid system for the hydraulic pump and an electric swing motor. This strategy adjusts the motor-generator power based on the required pump power. Similarly, in [9], various rulebased control strategies were designed for a parallel hybrid wheel loader. These strategies were evaluated in simulations in terms of fuel efficiency and achieved a 3–13% reduction in fuel consumption compared to a conventional wheel loader. Rule-based control strategies have also been validated in real-world operations. In [10], a prototype hybrid excavator with a parallel hybrid system for the pump and an electric swing motor was developed. A rule-based control strategy was implemented and tested in this prototype excavator. Rule-based strategies are simple and have a low computational effort. However, they are typically optimized for a specific mission cycle and do not guarantee the same level of performance in real-world cycles. In contrast, optimization-based strategies introduce control objectives by defining cost functions to be optimized and thus providing proof of optimality. Dynamic Programming (DP) [11] is one of the most widely used techniques for global optimization. However, DP requires prior knowledge of the entire cycle, and its high computational burden makes real-time energy management highly challenging. In [12], a rule-based control strategy for a hybrid excavator was developed by analyzing the results of a DP-based control strategy. Furthermore, DP is also used as a benchmark strategy [13], [14]. Control strategies based on Pontryagin's Minimum Principle (PMP) are strong candidates for real-time capable control strategies. The application of the Equivalent Consumption Minimization Strategy (ECMS) to off-highway hybrid machines has been widely documented in the literature [13], [14], [15]. In [13], an ECMS-based energy management strategy was implemented in a hybrid excavator equipped with an electric swing motor. Test results with the real vehicle demonstrated approximately 30% reduction in fuel consumption compared to a conventional excavator. PMP-based strategies require lower computational effort but cannot handle discrete states, such as mode transitions and gear shifts, within their control framework. To address this limitation, the authors of [16] combined DP and PMP to derive the optimal startstop sequence of the internal combustion engine (ICE) for plug-in electric vehicles. Their simulations confirmed that the DP-PMP algorithm yields near-optimal performance. Other studies [17], [18], [19] extended this approach to optimize both ICE start-stop and gear shifting for on-highway hybrid vehicles. However, to the best of the authors' knowledge, DP-PMP-based energy management strategies have not yet been validated through real-world testing. Furthermore, their application is limited to on-highway vehicles so far. In this paper, we propose a DP-PMP-based control algorithm as a real-time energy management strategy for a hybrid wheel loader. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

list-item.p: We adapt the DP-PMP approach to off-highway hybrid powertrains and formulate an energy management algorithm.
We present the control architecture, including support functions, to ensure real-time implementation of the developed algorithm.
We evaluate control performance in terms of fuel consumption in both simulation and real-world testing.

sec.p: Additionally, we assess the real-time capability of the controller. The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section II presents the developed hybrid powertrain and the investigated mission cycles. Section III describes the modeling of key powertrain components for the implementation of an optimal control strategy. Section IV details the adopted optimal control algorithm, the controller design, and its implementation in the prototype hybrid wheel loader. The developed control algorithm is evaluated through simulations in Section V and validated via real-world testing in Section VI. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper.

sec.label: A.
sec.title: CONVENTIONAL POWERTRAIN
sec.p: A conventional 7-ton class wheel loader depicted in Fig. 1 is used as a baseline for research. The powertrain of the conventional wheel loader consists of three sub-systems:

list-item.p: POWER SOURCE The baseline wheel loader is powered by a 3.6 L, 4-cylinder Diesel internal combustion engine (ICE) with a maximum

sec.p: Y. Kakichi et al.: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader
2 VOLUME 14, 2026

power of 74.4 kW. The ICE is equipped with a Diesel Oxidation Catalyst (DOC) and a Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) system for exhaust gas aftertreatment. The ICE drives two hydraulic pumps connected to the engine output shaft. On the other side, a hydraulic pump for cooling fan is also connected.

list-item.p: WORKING HYDRAULIC SYSTEM A hydraulic pump with fixed displacement driven by the ICE provides hydraulic oil flow to the valve system. There are four cylinders in the hydraulic system, namely two steering cylinders, one tilt cylinder and one lift cylinder. The lift and tilt cylinders enable a wide range of work with various attachments. The most typical attachment is a bucket used for moving gravel, rocks, and other materials, but other attachments such as forklift, timber grapple, snowplow, sweeper roller and material handling arm are also used for special purposes [20]. The steering system is a so-called articulated steering system. The relative yaw angle between the front and rear part of the vehicle is changed by two hydraulic cylinders, allowing the vehicle to be significantly more maneuverable than a vehicle with coordinated steering [21], [22]. The steering wheel column is connected to the orbitrol, which supplies oil proportional to the amount of steering wheel rotation to the steering cylinders in the desired direction. The priority valve supplies the required oil to the steering cylinders first, giving priority to steering for safety reasons. The remaining oil is supplied to the open center control valve, where the direction and flow rate are controlled by the spools.

PROPULSION SYSTEM A hydraulic pump with variable displacement driven by the ICE forms a hydrostatic transmission (HST) together with a variable displacement hydraulic motor. All four wheels are mechanically connected to the output shaft of the hydraulic motor, enabling all-wheel drive functionality. There is a hydraulically actuated two-speed transmission between the HST output shaft and the cardan shaft. With the second gear, high-speed driving up to 36 km/h is possible.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: MISSION CYCLES
sec.p: Wheel loaders cover a wide range of work, and their applications are versatile. Among others, the most common and widely studied [23], [24], [25] wheel loader cycle is a loading cycle, also called a V-cycle because of the shape of the vehicle movement. Fig. 2 presents a schematic top view of the V-cycle, while the top two subplots in Fig. 3 show the measured vehicle speed and cylinder stroke during the V-cycle. In this cycle, a wheel loader loads materials such as soil, gravel and sand into a load receiver, which is typically a truck placed next to a pile of material. The V-cycle can be divided into four parts. In phase A, the wheel loader moves forward to a pile of material and fills the bucket with material. In phase B, the vehicle drives backwards and returns to the starting point. In this phase, the bucket's position remains

caption.p: Schematic top view of the V-cycle.

sec.p: almost unchanged. In phase C, the vehicle steers slightly and moves forward towards the load receiver. While driving forward, the bucket is raised by extending the lift cylinder. After stopping the vehicle in front of the load receiver, the tilt cylinder is extended to empty the bucket. Finally, in phase D, the vehicle reverses and returns to the starting point. The bucket is lowered by contracting the lift cylinder while driving backwards. The series of phase A to D is repeated several times until the load receiver is full of material.

The bottom two subplots in Fig. 3 compare the requested hydraulic flow rate with the actual supply from the hydraulic pump. There is a large gap between the supplied flow rate and the requested flow rate, especially during phase A and phase B, as marked by red arrows in Fig. 3. In these phases, the bucket is moved only slightly, resulting in a low requested flow rate. However, since the hydraulic pump is connected to the same ICE output shaft as the HST, it is driven at high speeds when the operator presses the accelerator pedal to drive the vehicle. As a result, the hydraulic pump generates an unnecessarily large amount of oil flow within the hydraulic system, which returns to the tank without doing useful hydraulic work. The key to reducing hydraulic losses from the operational perspective is, therefore, to keep the pump speed as close as possible to the speed required for the requested hydraulic flow rate. Another mission cycle considered in this paper is a combination of the V-cycle with short driving, as shown in Fig. 4. This combined cycle serves as a more realistic mission cycle in a quarry. After five repetitions of the V-cycle (marked as 1 in Fig. 4), the wheel loader transports material to another location to increase productivity instead of simply waiting for another truck to arrive at the loading area. First, the bucket is loaded (2 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives with a full bucket (3 in Fig. 4). After transportation, the bucket is emptied (4 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives the same route with an empty bucket (5 in Fig. 4) to return to

sec.label: C.
sec.title: PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM
sec.p: The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1 has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5 shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid system for a wheel loader.

The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both parallel and series topologies. In this configuration, the ICE is not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located between the P2 EM and the ICE.

The hydraulic drivetrain has been electrified with two electric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic motors have higher torque density compared to electric motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each electric drive unit (EDU) to fulfill the maximum vehicle speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle speeds. sec.label: D.
sec.title: OPERATOR INTERFACE AND OPERATING STRATEGIES
sec.p: FOR PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired hydraulic flow rate from the pump or to get the desired propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:

list-item.p: Low efficiency in the working hydraulic system: Since the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess flow.

High operator workload: As the ICE drives both working hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position influences the pump flow rate and the propulsion torque. This means that the values controlled by the operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration – must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joystick and brake pedal.

caption.p: shows the new operator interface developed for

sec.p: the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed and propulsion torque.

Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the workinghydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used to determine the propulsion torque. The electrified propulsion system also offers the possibility of recuperating the kinetic energy of the vehicle, which in conventional vehicles would be lost as heat through mechanical brakes, through regenerative braking. By calibrating the target propulsion to a negative value at a low pedal position, the operator can decelerate the vehicle by releasing the accelerator pedal. In addition to efficiency benefits, this operating strategy facilitates one-

The pump speed in hybrid wheel loader is controlledby the P2 EM, not by the ICE in the conventional wheel loader for the following two reasons. Firstly, the ICE is not always connected to the pump. In full electric operation, the ICE is disconnected from the pump and cannot control the pump speed. The target EM speed nEM,tar is therefore calculated based on the required pump speed npump,req, while the ICE receives the target torque rather than the target speed.

The main disadvantage of DP is its high computationaleffort. Due to the two-dimensional state grid in this problem, implementing this control policy in a real vehicle controller is highly challenging. In this paper, the classical DP problem is modified into DP-PMP [16], [17], [18], [19] to enable realtime implementation of ICE start-stop and torque control. In particular, the sub-problem of determining the optimal ICE torque in hybrid mode is separated from the DP formulation. Instead, the Pontryagin's Minimum Principle (PMP) is applied to reduce the dimensionality of the state grid.
As a result, the optimal energy management problem isdivided into two parts as follows.

list-item.p: DP is used to optimize the ICE stat-stop decision.
PMP is used to determine the optimal torque split between the ICE and the electric machine.

sec.title: CONTROLLER DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION OF THE
sec.p: DP-PMP-BASED OPTIMAL ENERGY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY The optimization algorithm based on DP-PMP requires future cycle information, such as the pump flow rate, pressure, and EDU power.

Compared to on-highway vehicles, predicting future powerdemands of off-highway vehicles is more complicated, as it depends not only on the speed profile but also on factors such as the interaction of the power take-offs (PTOs) with the boundary conditions. One feature of off-highway mission cycles that simplifies the prediction of power demands is their repetitiveness. The power demand prediction in this paper assumes that wheel loaders follow repetitive daily mission cycles, as they operate within a limited work area, such as a quarry. The main idea is to use previously performed mission cycles for predicting future power demands. As described in Section II, mission cycles are divided into smaller segments, referred to as ''states'' in this paper. The prediction of power/flow demand is based on the set of states expected to be performed in the future.

In order to speed up the optimization calculation and makethe control strategy real-time implementable, the number of cost-to-go calculations in the DP algorithm is reduced by introducing a state-based optimization approach. This approach assumes that the ICE state does not change during each phase, and that the ICE start-stop events occur only when the state changes. The state-based ICE state optimization not only reduces the computational effort but also ensures minimal operating time of the ICE and thus avoids frequent start-stop events.

sec.p: cedure via DP-PMP. DP is applied to the ICE start-stop optimization problem on a state basis. By minimizing the cost-to-go function from the end of the prediction horizon to the start, the optimized ICE state at each predicted state is obtained. In the next step, the battery SOC is calculatedby forward simulation, using the optimal ICE state and precalculated ICE torque. This forward battery SOC calculation is done on a time basis. If the battery SOC at the end of the prediction horizon does not meet the specified termination criterion, the equivalence factor is updated. These steps are repeated with the updated equivalence factor until the terminal battery SOC condition is met. Finally, the optimal ICE state for each state and the optimal equivalence factor are obtained as the output of the calculation.

Based on the controller architecture described above, several operational constraints are inherently enforced to ensure robust and real-time operation. As summarized in Table 2, SOC bounds and hardware power limits are respected during operation, while ICE start–stop decisions are constrained to discrete vehicle state transitions. While the state-based formulation reduces start–stop toggling as an outcome, it also serves as an explicit operational constraint by enforcing a minimum on/off duration at the vehicle-state level. Thermal behavior is handled by restricting operation to the validated thermal operating envelope of the demonstrator to preserve real-time feasibility.

sec.label: V.
sec.title: SIMULATIVE INVESTIGATIONS
sec.p: In this section, the DP-PMP-based control strategy is compared with the rule-based control strategy through simulations of two different driving cycles. The first driving cycle is a V-cycle repeated ten times. The prediction horizon encompasses one loading cycle, which consists of four phases.

The second driving cycle is the combined cycle introducedin Section II. This cycle includes five repetitions of the V-cycle, followed by a bucket loading phase, driving with a loaded bucket, a bucket emptying phase, and driving with an empty bucket. It is assumed that all future scenarios, along with the power/flow demands of the first loading cycle and the first two drive states, are known a priori. The power/flow demand for each state in the prediction horizon is overwritten once that state is completed.

The rule-based control strategy adopted in this paper shiftsthe ICE torque to more fuel-efficient operating points while maintaining the battery SOC close to the target value [32]. The rule-based ICE start-stop control uses the total vehicle power demand to switch off the ICE, with a calibratable turnoff delay time. The turn-off power threshold and turn-off

sec.p: To compare the energy flow in the powertrain and to illustrate efficiency improvements, a Sankey diagram of the hybrid wheel loader in the V-cycle with both control strategies is presented in Fig. 16. The values in bold after arrowsrepresent the contributions of DP-PMP, while the remaining values pertain to the rule-based strategy. The values of DP- PMP are normalized to the fuel power of the rule-based strategy. Consequently, the EDU work, recuperation, auxiliary work, and effective hydraulic work remain consistent with those of the rule-based strategy. It is evident that DP- PMP reduces losses in the hydraulic system, and for the same amount of hydraulic work, the necessary input to the hydraulic pump decreased from 17.3% to 15.7% of the fuel power of the rule-based strategy. Although the efficiency of P2 EM decreases slightly due to operation at lower speeds in electric mode – resulting in a slight increase in input power from the ICE (from 21.3% to 21.9% for the same battery charging power) – the reduction in hydraulic losses outweighs this effect. Consequently, the total power demand on the ICE is reduced from 38.6% to 37.6%. Furthermore, the ICE efficiency increases from 38.6% to 38.9%, resulting in an overall fuel consumption benefit of 3.3%.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: COMBINED-CYCLE

caption.p: shows the simulation results for the combined cycle. With the rule-based strategy, the ICE is switched off during driving if the total electrical power demand is below the threshold for a predefined time. The ICE turn-off delay time is calibrated to ensure that the ICE is not switched off during the V-cycle. Consequently, the benefit of electric operation in the rule-based strategy is quite limited due to the delayed turn-off of the ICE while driving. The battery SOC with the DP-PMP based strategy differs significantly from that of the rule-based strategy. Using future power/flow demand predictions, the controller aims to increase the battery SOC during the loading phases to enable electric driving. Consequently, even higher ICE torque is required in hybrid mode than in the V-cycle test case, resulting in the ICE operating points reaching even lower BSFC areas. Electric operation during driving substantially reduces fuel consumption. While driving, only a small amount of hydraulic flow is required for steering. Therefore, by switching off the ICE and operating the hydraulic pump at lower speeds, excessive hydraulic oil flow can be avoided. In the simulation results, it can be observed that three out of four drive states are electric, with the only hybrid drive occurring during a high-power-demand drive state (Drive B). Fig. 18 illustrates a comparison of the operating points of the ICE during the combined cycle. The ICE torque of the rule-based strategy is lower than that of the optimizationbased strategy. It can be observed that the optimization-based strategy operates the ICE around its best efficiency torque at the required pump speed and the time share of electric operation is significantly higher compared to that of rule-based strategy. In other words, the DP-PMP based strategy efficiently discharges the battery by switching off the ICE and increases the ICE efficiency in hybrid mode to compensate for the battery energy discharge. sec.label: VII.
sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: This paper has presented a novel real-time capable energy management strategy based on the DP-PMP algorithm for a hybrid wheel loader. To enable real-time implementation, wheel loader mission cycles were divided into small segments, and a future power demand prediction algorithm based on the repetitiveness of the mission cycles was introduced. Additionally, the timing of the ICE start-stop control decision was changed from the conventional time-based approach to machine state changes in order to further reduce the computational effort and to avoid unnecessary ICE start-stop events.

The developed energy management algorithm was testedin a simulation environment, and the simulation results confirmed that the proposed strategy can reduce fuel consumption by 3.3% in the V-cycle and 4.0% in the combined cycle.

A detailed analysis of the powertrain energy flow hasshown that the optimization-based control strategy reduces losses in the hydraulic system by reducing the pump speed in electric mode and uses the ICE more efficiently in areas with lower BSFC. The test results with the demonstrator con- firmed that the required time for the optimization calculation is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, proving that the proposed strategy is capable of real-time operation. The test results with the hybrid wheel loader confirmed that the presented control strategy can improve the BSFC of the ICE in both the V-cycle and the combined cycle by using the ICE in areas with higher efficiency. However, due to the varying workloads during testing, it is difficult to evaluate the overall fuel consumption benefits.

The proposed approach relies on correct state detectionto trigger optimization based on predicted power demand. In practical implementation, when state detection confidence is insufficient or misclassification is detected, the controller intentionally disables the DP–PMP optimization and falls back to a conservative baseline strategy, such as a rulebased controller or adaptive ECMS. This fallback mechanism ensures robust and safe operation under uncertain or unforeseen conditions, while preserving the benefits of optimization when reliable predictions are available.

Future research could focus on analyzing the potentialfor reducing raw pollutant emissions through reduced transient ICE operation, thanks to hybridization. Furthermore, the integration of emission control into the optimization control framework to investigate the optimal concept for exhaust aftertreatment systems is another area for future studies. In addition, the provision of future scenarios through the networking of machines and their management as a fleet on the construction site is another research focus.
